title: Tikam Singh vs . on 15 January, 2010
full_text: Tikam Singh vs . on 15 January, 2010 1 IN THE COURT OF SH. VIVEK KUMAR GULIA METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE ­ 1 [East] KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI In the matter of: Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh C.C. No. 3924/07 PS: Bhajanpura JUDGMENT 1. The serial number of the case : 45/2005 2. The date of complaint : 21.03.2005 3. Name of the complainant : Tikam Singh S/o. Sh. Budh Prakash, R/o. Mohalla Ratan Nagar, (Near Romesh Cinema) Baghpat Road, Meerut, UP. 4. The name, parentage Birbal Singh, and residence of accused : S/o. Sh. Bhola Shanker, R/o. H. No. C­265/B, Gali No.10, Bhajanpura, Delhi. 5. Offence complained of : U/s. 138 N. I. Act . 6. Plea of the accused : Pleaded not guilty. 7. Final Order : Acuitted. 8. Case reserved for order : 12.01.2010. 9. Date of such order : 15.01.2010. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 2 REASONS FOR THE DECISION: 1. The accused was put to trial as a result present complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (in short 'the Act'). The facts of the case, in nutshell, are these. It is the complaint's case that Rs. two lacs was borrowed by accused from the complainant on 21.06.2004 and in discharge of his legal liability, accused handed over a cheque bearing No. 734199 dt. 21.06.2004 for Rs. 2,00,000/­, drawn on Punjab National Bank, Yamuna Vihar, Delhi, but on presentation, the same was returned back unpaid with remarks 'Insufficient Funds'. Thereafter, legal notice dated 24.01.2005 was issued to accused who refused to accept it. Therefore, the accused, as he failed to make the payment within stipulated period, has committed an offence punishable under section 138 of the Act and u/s. 420 IPC. With aforesaid facts, complainant prayed for prosecution and punishment of accused in accordance with law. 2. Substance of accusation in the form of written notice u/s 251 Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 ( Cr.P.C .) was read over and explained to accused on 18.07.2006, to which he pleaded not Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 3 guilty and claimed trial. 3. In post summoning evidence, complainant stepped into witness box as CW1 and reiterated the facts mentioned in the complaint by way of his affidavit and proved the documents, i.e., cheque in question Ex.CW1/A, memo regarding presentation of the cheque for encashment Ex.CW1/B, cheque returning memo dt. 23.12.04 EX.CW1/B1, cheque returning memo dt. 20.12.04 EX.CW1/C, legal notice dt. 24.01.2005 EX.CW1/D, Regd. Post receipt dt. 27.01.2005 EX.CW1/D1, UPC receipt dt. 27.01.2005 EX.CW1/D2, envelop (returned back) EX.CW1/D3 and AD card EX.CW1/D4. 4. CW2, Rajender Singh, Manager, PNB, Bhajanpura, proved the relevant entries of cheque returning register as Ex. CW2/1 and cheque returning memo EX.CW1/C. 5. CW3, Baldev Singh, Clerk, Syndicate Bank, Baghpat Road, Meerut, proved the relevant entry in collection register as Ex. CW3/1. 6. A. S. Medhavi (CW4), Clerk, Syndicate Bank, Meerut, Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 4 stated on oath as per records, cheque returning memo dated 23.12.2004 (?) issued by PNB, Delhi, was handed over to complainant on 04.01.2005. It is mentioned that inadvertently original acknowledgment receipt was given to complainant which is already Ex. CW1/B1. 7. Accused was questioned generally about the case put forward by the complainant against him and his statement was recorded U/s. 313 Cr. P. C., wherein it is stated that cheque in question was not issued by him in discharge of any legal liability. It is explained that cheque book containing the cheque in question was lost and complainant misused the same. Further, it is mentioned that all the entries in the cheque in question except the signature have not filled up by him. 8. Accused showed his willingness to lead defence evidence but failed to adduce evidence in any form and ultimately he closed defence evidence on 18.03.2009. 9. I have heard the Bar and perused the record. 10. The most emphasized defensive plea of accused is that Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 5 cheque in question was not issued in favour of the complainant. It is alleged that the signed cheque was misplaced and same has been misused by the complainant. It is also argued that accused has no direct relation with the complainant and cheque being without any consideration, complaint case be dismissed. However, it can be seen that except the word of the mouth of accused, there is not an iota of evidence on record to suggest that cheque was not issued by accused in favour of complainant to discharge his liability. There is no explanation as to from where the cheque was misplaced and how it came into the hands of complainant. Further, why any report to police authorities or bank was not given is not made clear. In brief, no ocular or documentary evidence has been produced to substantiate the plea taken by accused. During cross­examination of complainant (CW1), it came on record that both the parties used to visit the house of one Gajender Singh Sangwan at Meerut and since accused was in need of money for making a bid in tender for scraps, cheque amount was given to him on interest @ 2% p.m. It is mentioned that cheque was handed over on 21.06.2004 and no loan agreement was executed between the parties. Further, complainant denied the suggestion of accused that cheque book signed by accused was misplaced and blank cheque in question Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 6 was misused. Thus, it becomes clear that complainant has withstood the test of cross­examination and accused failed to bring anything on record to demolish the case of complainant. 11. Another issue raised by defence side is pertaining to service of legal notice. It is contended that the statutory legal notice was not served on accused, therefore, complaint is liable to dismissed. It is contended that postal endorsement "suchna de di gai hai (information given)" dt. 29.01.05 cannot be considered to be deemed service on accused in absence of report as to where and to whom the intimation was given by the postman. In my view, this plea of accused is without any substance. When his address has not been disputed by accused, there can not be any doubt that intimation about the regd. post envelop was given to addressee or his family member at the address mentioned thereon. Further, on this issue, it has been categorically held by Supreme Court in the case of K. Bhaskaran Vs. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan cited as (1999) 7 SCC 510 that : "...Thus, when a notice is returned by the sendee as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in clause (c) to the proviso of section 138 of the Act. Of course, such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 7 drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address. In the present case the accused did not even attempt to discharge the burden to rebut the aforesaid presumption". Further, it has been laid down in re: Bhaskaran Vs. Betan (1999) 3 Ker LT 440; Joseph Jose Vs. J Baby 2002 Cr.LJ 4392 (Ker) that : "The endorsement 'unclaimed' can be taken as refusal. Sending of notice to the correct address of the accused and return of the same with endorsement 'unclaimed' are sufficient for the purpose of due compliance of sec. 138 (b) . Burden to prove non­tender of the article is on the accused." In view of these case­laws, there remains no doubt that accused was required to discharge the burden to rebut the legal presumption of deemed service of legal notice on him, but no effort was made by him in this regard. 12. Another point raised from defence side is relating to privity of contract between the parties. It is contended that the complainant failed to prove his relationship with accused and therefore, no question arises as to borrowing money from him. In this regard, it can be observed that complainant has named one Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 8 Gajender Singh, at whose house parties used to meet, in his cross­examination. Accused has not denied this fact by way of any suggestion. Moreover, the burden was on accused to rebut the fact that the complainant had acquaintance with him and same has not been discharged. Thus, this ground of argument also fails. 13. The complainant case was also challenged on the ground that since the entries on the cheque in question except the signatures are not in the handwriting of accused, it gives strength to the defence plea that the complainant has misused the cheque. After carefully examining the cheque in question, it appears to me that all the entries except the name of payee have been filled up by the same person. Since the signatures on the cheque in question has not been disputed by accused, it can be concluded that the amount and date columns have also been completed by him only. As far as the name of payee is concerned, there is no legal requirement that same should be in the handwriting of drawer of the cheque. Moreover, no effort has been made by the accused to prove that the entries of the cheque in question are not in his handwriting. Thus, this objection also deserves dismissal. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 9 14. Lastly, it is vehemently argued that complaint has not been filed within limitation period. In this regard, two objections have been raised. Firstly, it is contended that the legal notice has been sent to accused after expiration of statutory period of 30 days and secondly, the complaint was filed in the court after expiry of limitation period of one month. To decide this aspect of the matter, the relevant events upto the filing of the complaint are summarized as under:  Cheque presented for encashment ­ 14.12.2004.  Cheque returned unpaid by banker of accused (PNB) - 20.12.04.  Information sent to manager of complainant's bank at Baghpat from Delhi qua unpaid cheque ­ 23.12.04.  Legal notice dt. 24.01.05 dispatched ­ 27.01.05  Endorsement of "soochna de di gayi hai" made ­ 29.01.05.  Complaint filed on 16.03.2005. 15. As per section 138 of the Act, the payee is required to make a demand for the payment of cheque amount by giving a Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 10 notice in writing to the drawer of cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of cheque as unpaid and thereafter if drawer of the cheque fails to make payment within 15 days after receiving the said notice, offence under section 138 of the Act is deemed to have been committed. Further section 142 of the Act speaks that after non­payment, complaint is required to be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arose under clause (c) of the Proviso to sec. 138 of the Act. If we give conjoint reading to both the above mentioned provisions of the Act, then it can be concluded that the complaint has to be filed within one month after expiry of 15 days of the receipt of the notice by the drawer. 16. In regard to first objection, it can be observed that complainant witnesses have proved by way of oral and documentary evidence that the cheque returning memo was received by complainant on 04.01.2005 and therefore a legal notice was to be dispatched on or before 03.02.2005 (within 30 days). In the present case, the legal notice was posted on 27.01.2005. Therefore, the first objection raised on behalf of accused that statutory legal notice has not been sent within 30 Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 11 days after receiving the information as to dishonour of cheque is found to be baseless. 17. Second objection is pertaining to filing of complaint beyond limitation period of one month. It is argued by Ld. Counsel for complainant that though the endorsement (information given) was made by postman on 29.01.2005, however, the limitation period should be counted atleast 03 days after that as this time can be presumed to have been taken in giving that information to the complainant. On this point, Ld. Defence Counsel argued that the period of limitation is to be counted from the date of endorsement itself and in support of this plea, reliance is placed upon the judgment given by the High Court of Delhi in the case titled as Ashwani Kumar Julka v Lt. Col . Parthojit Choudhary (Retd.) 136 (2007) DLT 241. This judgment makes it clear that 15 days period is to be counted from the date of receipt of notice by the drawer of the cheque and not when the sender of the notice received the intimation. Therefore, in the case in hand, the 15 days period is to be counted from 29.01.2005 and thus it would expire on 13.02.2005. In this manner, cause of action for filing the present complaint arose from the next following day, i.e., 14.02.2005, Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 12 which has to be excluded being the first day. This is how the period of limitation is counted as explained by the Supreme Court judgment in case titled as M/s. Saketh India Ltd. and others v India Securities Ltd. 1999 CRI. L.J. 1822. 18. Further Ld. Defence Counsel pointed out that complaint has been filed within 30 days after accrual of cause of action and urged that even if the period of limitation of one month is counted w.e.f. 14.02.2005, the complaint can be said to have been filed within limitation period of one month since the month of February was having 28 days in the year 2005. Ld. Defence Counsel relied upon judgment of High Court of Delhi given in the case titled as Srikant Somani & Ors. Vs. Sharad Gupta & Anr. 2005 II AD (Cr.) DHC 520. 19. Clause (b) of section 142 of the Act mandates that a complaint is to be made within one month of the date of accrual of the cause of action. As such, it would be erroneous to say that a complaint is to be made within 30/31 days of the date of accrual of cause of action. "30 days" is not synonymous with one month and vice versa. How a one month is counted has been provided in Halsbury's Laws of England : Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 13 "When the period prescribed is a calendar month running from any arbitrary date, the period expires with the day in the succeeding month immediately preceding the day corresponding to the date upon which the period starts, save that, if the period starts at the end of a calendar month the period expires at the end of the latter month." In view of above settled position of law, period of limitation of one month starting w.e.f. 14.02.2005 expired on 14.03.2005. Therefore, manner of counting the limitation period suggested by counsel for accused is not in consonance with the law as propounded in the aforesaid decisions given by Supreme Court and the High Court. Even the judgment of the High Court relied upon by the Ld. Counsel for complainant makes it clear that the computation of the period of one month has to start on 15.02.2005 (first day being excluded) and the month from 15.02.2005 ends on 14.03.2005. Unfortunately, the complaint has been filed on 16.03.2005, i.e., two days after the expiry of limitation period. The complainant did not pray for condoning of the delay in filing the complaint. In the facts of the present case, court would generally be liberal in condoning the period of delay but in absence of an application, it is not permissible for this court to condone the delay [(2001) 9 SCC 717]. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07 14 20. The upshot of the discussion would be that the present complaint is time barred. In the result, the complaint is ordered to be dismissed. Accused is acquitted of the offence u/s. 138 of the Act. Announced in the open (Vivek Kumar Gulia) court on 15.01.2010 Metropolitan Magistrate­I(E) (total fourteen pages) Karkardooma Courts, Delhi. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; C.C. No. 3924/07
